name: Where are multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) used, and how do they perform on MNIST? Describe the MNIST benchmark, the deep-MLP result of Ciresan et al. (2010) and the idea of LeNet-1 (1998) with its output interpretation including rejection.
answer:
MLP applications. The MLP is the basic network used when it is unclear what topology is appropriate; it is often a component of large models, especially at the head of the network, interpreting features extracted by lower, more specialized layers. It was the most prominent NN architecture in the 80s and 90s (applications: ALVINN autonomous driving car, character/digit recognition, table data processing, …). Two-layer MLPs are usually not much better than non-neural models.

MNIST. Database of labelled images of handwritten digits: 60 000 training and 10 000 testing examples of size \(28\times28\) pixels, digits centred on the centre of gravity of pixel values and normalized to a fixed size. A standard benchmark that allows comparing methods.

Ciresan et al. 2010. A deep MLP with 784-2500-2000-1500-1000-500-10 neurons trained on a GPU with plain on-line backpropagation reached an error rate of about \(0.35\,\%\); the ingredients were many hidden layers, many neurons per layer, numerous deformed training images and graphics cards to speed up learning.

LeNet-1 (LeCun et al. 1998) – a famous learning convolutional network. Output interpretation: the output neuron with the highest value identifies the digit; with rejection, if the two largest output values are too close together the input is rejected (no answer), which lowers the error rate at the price of leaving some inputs unclassified. A dense MLP needed to reject more inputs than LeNet-1 to reach a comparable error.
keyPoints: MLP: default when topology unclear; head of large models; dominant in 80s–90s; 2-layer MLP ≈ non-neural models
MNIST: 60 000 train / 10 000 test, \(28\times28\), centred and size-normalized, standard benchmark
Ciresan 2010: deep wide MLP + deformed images + GPU → error about \(0.35\,\%\)
LeNet-1: argmax output; reject if the two largest outputs are too close
Rejection trades unclassified inputs for lower error; the convolutional net rejects less than a dense MLP
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 155–159 (slide 158 is the LeNet-1 figure; error figures reduced to the central one)

name: Explain the basic building blocks of a convolutional layer: local receptive field, stride length, feature map and weight sharing. Why do all neurons of a feature map share weights and biases, and why are several feature maps used in one layer?
answer:
Local receptive field. Every neuron of a convolutional layer is connected only to a field of \(k\times k\) neurons (e.g. \(5\times5\)) in the lower layer – its receptive field. The neuron itself is "standard": it computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies an activation function.
Stride length. The next neuron gets the receptive field slid over by some number of pixels (neurons), e.g. by one pixel to the right; the size of this slide is the stride length.
Feature map. The group of all neurons obtained by sliding the receptive field over the input is a feature map; all these neurons share weights and biases (they apply the same filter, but to different inputs).
Why sharing. Each feature map represents a property of the input that is supposed to be spatially invariant – the same feature (e.g. an edge) is detected in the same way wherever it occurs in the image. Sharing also drastically reduces the number of parameters, which allows very deep architectures.
Several feature maps. One map detects one property; typically several feature maps are used in a single layer to detect several properties (e.g. 20 maps with \(5\times5\) receptive fields).
keyPoints: Neuron connected to a \(k\times k\) receptive field; standard weighted sum + activation
Stride = size of the shift of the receptive field between neighbouring neurons
Feature map = all neurons from sliding the field; shared weights and bias
Each feature map detects a spatially invariant property
Several feature maps per layer for several properties; sharing reduces parameters and enables depth
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 161–165, 184 (slides 161–162, 165–166 are figures)

name: Practical: a simple convolutional network takes a \(28\times28\) input image. Its convolutional layer has 3 feature maps with \(5\times5\) receptive fields and stride 1; each feature map is followed by its own max-pooling map with \(2\times2\) fields and stride 2; 10 output neurons are fully connected to all pooling neurons. Compute (a) the size of each feature map and of each pooling map, (b) the number of trainable parameters of the convolutional layer, and compare it with a dense layer of the same number of neurons fully connected to the input, (c) the number of parameters of the output layer. Which layer has no parameters, and how is the network trained?
answer:
(a) A \(k\times k\) field with stride \(s\) on an \(N\times N\) input gives \(\frac{N-k}{s}+1\) positions per dimension: \(\frac{28-5}{1}+1=\mathbf{24}\), so the convolutional layer has \(3\times24\times24\) neurons. Max-pooling with \(2\times2\) fields and stride 2 (disjoint fields) halves each dimension: \(\mathbf{3\times12\times12}\).
(b) All neurons of a feature map share weights and bias: \(5\cdot5=25\) weights \(+\,1\) bias \(=26\) per map, \(\mathbf{78}\) for 3 maps. A dense layer with the same \(3\cdot24\cdot24=1728\) neurons, each connected to all 784 inputs, would need \(784\cdot1728+1728=\mathbf{1\,356\,480}\) parameters.
(c) Each of the 10 output neurons receives input from each of the \(3\cdot12\cdot12=432\) pooling neurons: \(10\cdot432=4320\) weights \(+\,10\) biases \(=\mathbf{4330}\).
The pooling layer has no weights: its neurons only compute a simple aggregate (max). The network is trained using backpropagation, which is easily adapted to convolutional networks (shared weights sum the gradient contributions of all their connections; max-pooling passes the gradient to the maximal input).
keyPoints: Feature map size \(\frac{28-5}{1}+1=24\) → \(3\times24\times24\)
\(2\times2\) / stride 2 pooling → \(3\times12\times12\)
Shared parameters: \(3\cdot(25+1)=78\) vs \(1\,356\,480\) for a dense layer
Output layer: \(10\cdot432+10=4330\) parameters
Pooling layers have no weights; training by backprop adapted to CNNs
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 161–164, 167, 177, 182–183. Slide 167's text says max-pooling with field 5x5 and stride 1, but its figure shows 3x24x24 -> 3x12x12, which corresponds to 2x2 pooling with stride 2; the prompt therefore states the pooling explicitly. The size formula and parameter counts are derived, not slide text.

name: What does a pooling layer compute? Give the definitions (and formulas where available) of max-pooling, L2-pooling and average pooling, state how pooling maps relate to feature maps, and compute all three for one pooling neuron whose \(2\times2\) receptive field contains the values 1, 3, 2, 0.
answer:
Neurons of a pooling layer are organized into pooling maps; all of them compute a simple aggregate function of their receptive field and have disjoint inputs; they have no weights. Pooling after convolution is usually applied to each feature map separately, i.e. a single pooling map after each feature map.
• Max-pooling: maximum of inputs, \(y_j=\max_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}y_i\).
• L2-pooling: square root of the sum of squares of the inputs, \(y_j=\sqrt{\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}y_i^2}\).
• Average pooling: mean, \(y_j=\dfrac{\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}y_i}{\lvert j_{\leftarrow}\rvert}\).
(\(j_{\leftarrow}\) is the set of neurons with an arc to \(j\).)
Example \((1,3,2,0)\): max \(=\mathbf3\); L2 \(=\sqrt{1+9+4+0}=\sqrt{14}\approx\mathbf{3.74}\); average \(=6/4=\mathbf{1.5}\).
keyPoints: Pooling neurons: aggregate function, disjoint inputs, no weights
One pooling map per feature map
Max: \(y_j=\max_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}y_i\)
L2: \(\sqrt{\sum y_i^2}\); average: \(\sum y_i/\lvert j_{\leftarrow}\rvert\)
Example: max 3, L2 \(\approx3.74\), average 1.5
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 164, 177, 179 (L2-pooling formula is the slide's verbal definition written out)

name: Define a convolutional network formally, focusing on what differs from an MLP: the layer types, the set \([ji]\) of connections sharing a weight, the activity of pooling neurons, and the error function.
answer:
The notation of MLPs is reused: \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) (input, output, all neurons), \(\xi_j\), \(y_j\), \(w_{ji}\) (weight of the connection from \(i\) to \(j\)), \(j_{\leftarrow}\), \(j_{\rightarrow}\), formal unit input \(y_0=1\), \(0\in j_{\leftarrow}\). (The slide writes the bias weight as \(w_{j0}=-b_j\); in these notes \(w_{j0}\) is simply the bias \(b_j\) – the two conventions differ only by the sign of \(b_j\).)

Architecture. Neurons are organized in layers \(L_0,L_1,\dots,L_n\) with connections (typically) only from \(L_m\) to \(L_{m+1}\). Layer types:
• input layer \(L_0\);
• dense layer – each neuron connected with each neuron of the previous layer;
• convolutional layer – neurons organized into disjoint feature maps; all neurons of a feature map share weights (but have different inputs);
• pooling layer – "neurons" organized into pooling maps, all computing a simple aggregate function (e.g. max) on disjoint inputs.
New notation: \([ji]\) is the set of all connections (pairs of neurons) sharing the weight \(w_{ji}\); in a dense layer \([ji]\) is a single connection.

Activity. Dense and convolutional neurons: \(\xi_j=\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}w_{ji}y_i\), \(y_j=\sigma_j(\xi_j)\) with an arbitrary differentiable \(\sigma_j\). Pooling neurons apply the pooling function (max: \(y_j=\max_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}y_i\); average: \(y_j=\frac{\sum_{i\in j_{\leftarrow}}y_i}{\lvert j_{\leftarrow}\rvert}\)). The network is evaluated layer-wise as an MLP; \(y_j(w,x)\) is the value of output neuron \(j\) for weights \(w\) and input \(x\).

Learning. Training set \(\{(x_k,d_k)\mid k=1,\dots,p\}\) and error \(E_k(w)=\frac12\sum_{j\in Y}(y_j(w,x_k)-d_{kj})^2\) as for MLPs. (The slide writes \(E=\sum_kE_k\); with \(E=\frac1p\sum_kE_k\) as in L3 only the scale of the learning rate changes.)
keyPoints: Layers \(L_0,\dots,L_n\), connections \(L_m\to L_{m+1}\); input, dense, convolutional, pooling layers
Conv: disjoint feature maps with shared weights; pooling: aggregate on disjoint inputs
\([ji]\) = set of connections sharing the weight \(w_{ji}\)
\(\xi_j=\sum w_{ji}y_i\), \(y_j=\sigma_j(\xi_j)\); pooling by max/avg; layer-wise evaluation
\(E_k=\frac12\sum_{j\in Y}(y_j-d_{kj})^2\); normalisation only rescales the learning rate
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 177–180 (shortened to the CNN-specific parts; slide 178 writes w_j0 = -b_j, slide 83 of L3 has w_j0 = b_j)

name: Derive backpropagation for convolutional networks. How is \(\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}\) obtained for a weight of a dense layer and for a shared weight of a convolutional layer? How are \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j\) computed for output neurons, for neurons followed by dense or convolutional layers, and for neurons followed by a max-pooling layer? Justify the shared-weight formula.
answer:
Step 1 – from weights to outputs.
• Dense layer (no shared weights): \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}=\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}\,\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\,y_i\).
• Convolutional layer: summing over all connections \((r,s)\) that share the weight \(w_{ji}\), \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial w_{ji}}=\sum_{(r,s)\in[ji]}\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\,\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\,y_s. \] Justification: the shared weight occurs in the inner potential \(\xi_r=\dots+w_{ji}y_s+\dots\) of every neuron \(r\) with a connection \((r,s)\in[ji]\); \(E_k\) depends on \(w_{ji}\) through all of them, so by the chain rule the derivative is the sum of the per-connection contributions \(\frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\cdot\frac{\partial y_r}{\partial\xi_r}\cdot\frac{\partial\xi_r}{\partial w_{ji}}\) with \(\frac{\partial\xi_r}{\partial w_{ji}}=y_s\).
• Neurons of pooling layers have no weights.
Step 2 – derivatives w.r.t. outputs (from the output layer downwards, as in an MLP):
• \(j\in Y\): \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=y_j-d_{kj}\) (for the squared error; other error functions give a different derivative).
• \(j\in Z\setminus Y\) whose successors \(j_{\rightarrow}\) form a dense or convolutional layer: \(\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_r}\,\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\,w_{rj}\).
• \(j\in Z\setminus Y\) whose successor is a max-pooling neuron: \(j_{\rightarrow}=\{i\}\) for a single "max" neuron, and \[ \frac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_j}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\partial E_k}{\partial y_i}&j=\arg\max_{r\in i_{\leftarrow}}y_r,\\[2mm] 0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} \] – the gradient flows only to the input that attained the maximum.
keyPoints: Dense: \(\partial E_k/\partial w_{ji}=\partial E_k/\partial y_j\cdot\sigma_j'(\xi_j)\cdot y_i\)
Conv: sum over \((r,s)\in[ji]\) of \(\partial E_k/\partial y_r\cdot\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\cdot y_s\) (chain rule over all uses of the shared weight)
Pooling neurons have no weights
Output: \(\partial E_k/\partial y_j=y_j-d_{kj}\) (squared error)
Hidden before dense/conv: \(\sum_{r\in j_{\rightarrow}}\partial E_k/\partial y_r\cdot\sigma_r'(\xi_r)\cdot w_{rj}\)
Before max-pooling: gradient copied to the argmax input, 0 to the others
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 182–183 (the chain-rule justification of the shared-weight sum spells out the slide formula)

name: Practical: (a) A one-dimensional convolutional layer with the shared kernel \((w_1,w_2)=(0.5,-1)\), no bias and identity activation is applied with stride 1 to the input \(x=(1,2,3)\), giving two output neurons \(y_1,y_2\). With desired outputs \(d=(-1,-1)\) and squared error \(E=\frac12\sum_j(y_j-d_j)^2\), compute \(y_1,y_2\), \(\partial E/\partial w_1\) and \(\partial E/\partial w_2\). (b) A max-pooling neuron \(i\) has inputs \(y=(0.2,0.9,0.5,0.1)\) and the backpropagated derivative \(\partial E/\partial y_i=-0.3\). Compute \(\partial E/\partial y_j\) for its four inputs.
answer:
(a) Forward: \(y_1=0.5\cdot1+(-1)\cdot2=\mathbf{-1.5}\); \(y_2=0.5\cdot2+(-1)\cdot3=\mathbf{-2}\). Output derivatives (squared error): \(\partial E/\partial y_1=y_1-d_1=-0.5\), \(\partial E/\partial y_2=y_2-d_2=-1\). With identity activation \(\sigma'=1\). The weight \(w_1\) is shared by the connections \(x_1\to y_1\) and \(x_2\to y_2\), so \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_1}=(-0.5)\cdot x_1+(-1)\cdot x_2=(-0.5)\cdot1+(-1)\cdot2=\mathbf{-2.5}. \] The weight \(w_2\) is shared by \(x_2\to y_1\) and \(x_3\to y_2\): \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial w_2}=(-0.5)\cdot2+(-1)\cdot3=\mathbf{-4}\). (Gradient descent would therefore increase both weights.)
(b) Only the input attaining the maximum (0.9, the second one) receives the derivative: \(\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial y}=(\mathbf0,\mathbf{-0.3},\mathbf0,\mathbf0)\).
keyPoints: Shared weight: sum contributions over all connections using it
\(\partial E/\partial w_1=-0.5\cdot1+(-1)\cdot2=-2.5\)
\(\partial E/\partial w_2=-0.5\cdot2+(-1)\cdot3=-4\)
Max-pooling: \((0,-0.3,0,0)\) – gradient only to the argmax
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 182–183; numeric example constructed to apply the slide formulas

name: Describe the convolutional network that classifies MNIST with only 33 errors on the 10 000 test images: its architecture, activation and output functions, error function and training setup. Explain the purpose of each training technique used (minibatch SGD, L2 regularization, dropout, dataset expansion, committee voting).
answer:
Architecture. Two convolutional-pooling layers – the first with 20, the second with 40 feature maps – followed by two dense (MLP) layers of 1000 neurons each and 10 outputs. Feature maps and dense layers use ReLU, pooling is max-pooling, the output layer is softmax. Error function: negative log-likelihood (= cross-entropy).
Training. SGD with minibatch size 10 and learning rate 0.03; L2 regularization with "weight" \(\lambda=0.1\) plus dropout with probability \(\frac12\); 40 epochs (every training example considered 40 times); expanded dataset: displacement by one pixel in an arbitrary direction; committee voting of 5 networks. Result: only 33 of the 10 000 test images misclassified.
Purposes (from the earlier lectures): minibatch SGD – cheap, noisy gradient estimates and many updates per epoch; L2 regularization (weight decay) and dropout – regularization against overfitting (dropout trains a large ensemble of thinned networks); dataset expansion by small shifts – more training data and invariance to small displacements; committee voting – an ensemble of networks whose combined vote reduces errors of individual models; softmax + cross-entropy – probabilistic outputs and a well-behaved gradient for classification (\(\partial E_k/\partial\xi_i=y_i-d_{ki}\)).
keyPoints: 2 conv-pool layers (20, 40 maps), dense 1000-1000, 10 outputs
ReLU, max-pooling, softmax output, negative log-likelihood = cross-entropy
SGD with minibatches, L2 regularization and dropout against overfitting
Dataset expanded by 1-pixel shifts; committee of 5 networks
Only 33 of 10 000 test errors
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 169–170; the purposes of the techniques refer back to earlier lectures and are explanation, not slide text

name: How did convolutional networks develop beyond MNIST? Describe ImageNet and the ILSVRC challenge (what is classified and the top-5 criterion with its rationale), the GoogLeNet and ResNet milestones, the main application areas of CNNs, and the summary characteristics of convolutional networks.
answer:
ImageNet is a large database of colour images in thousands of classes. ILSVRC (ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge): classification over a subset of ImageNet (1000 classes, over a million training images), started in 2010; it helped to trigger the breakthrough in image recognition. Because many images contain more than one object, the model may output five classes and the correct label must be among them (top-5 criterion).
Milestones. 2014: GoogLeNet, a deep convolutional network with 22 layers. 2015: ResNet, the winner with 152 layers; its skip connections implement residual learning – a layer adds its output to its input, which makes very deep networks trainable.
Applications: image classification (binary or many classes, 2D, 3D, … nD "images", movies), image segmentation (partitioning pixels – U-Net, fully convolutional networks and many other variants), object detection (bounding-box prediction, R-CNN architectures).
Summary: CNNs are nowadays the most used networks in image processing and in other areas whose input has local, spatially invariant properties (vision transformers are gradually taking over); they are typically trained by gradient descent and its modifications (e.g. Adam); thanks to weight sharing they allow (very) deep architectures; they are typically extended with further adjustments and tricks in their topologies.
keyPoints: ImageNet / ILSVRC: classification of 1000 classes, from 2010; drove the breakthrough in image recognition
Top-5 criterion because images often contain several objects
GoogLeNet 2014: 22 layers; ResNet 2015: 152 layers, skip connections (residual learning)
Applications: classification, segmentation (U-Net), object detection (R-CNN)
Most used in image processing; trained by GD variants (Adam); weight sharing enables depth; vision transformers rising
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 171–175, 184 (slide 174 contains a ResNet figure; the one-line explanation of residual learning is general knowledge)

name: A team trains a CNN to detect cancer in whole-slide images (WSI) of tissue, annotated by pathologists. Describe how the input data are prepared and labelled, how the training data are augmented and sampled, which network is used and how it is adapted, and the training setup (error function, optimizer, learning-rate and stopping rules). Explain why these choices make sense.
answer:
Data. A WSI is far too large to be processed at once (on the order of \(10^{5}\times10^{5}\) pixels), so it is cut into patches of \(512\times512\) px. A patch is labelled positive iff its inner square intersects the annotation; the annotations by pathologists are not pixel-level precise.
Augmentation: random vertical and horizontal flips, random colour perturbations. Three-step sampling of training data: 1. randomly select a label, 2. randomly select a slide containing at least one patch with that label, 3. randomly select a patch with the label from that slide (interpretation: this balances the classes and the contribution of individual slides).
Network. VGG16 (\(3\times3\) convolutions, \(2\times2\) max-pooling), pretrained on ImageNet; the top fully connected part is removed and replaced by global max-pooling and a single dense layer with a single logistic output – the probability of cancer in the patch. Error: cross-entropy.
Training: an optimizer with adaptive learning rates (RMSprop) plus momentum; if the validation error does not improve for a few consecutive epochs, the learning rate is halved; if the ROC AUC on validation data does not improve for a few more epochs, training terminates.
Why (interpretation): patches make the huge images tractable; flips and colour perturbations add invariances the diagnosis should have; pretrained weights transfer generic visual features; a logistic output with cross-entropy suits binary classification; learning-rate halving and early stopping on validation data are standard schedule and regularization techniques.
keyPoints: WSI too large → \(512\times512\) patches; positive iff inner square intersects the (imprecise) annotation
Augmentation: flips, colour perturbations; 3-step sampling: label → slide → patch
VGG16 pretrained on ImageNet; top FC replaced by global max-pooling + single dense logistic output
Cross-entropy error; RMSprop with momentum
Halve the learning rate when validation error stalls; stop when validation ROC AUC stalls
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 185–190 (slides 185–187, 189 contain figures; dataset sizes and hyperparameter values omitted; the "why" paragraph is interpretation)

name: Practical: the patch classifier \(F\) predicts a patch \(I\) positive iff \(F(I)\ge0.75\). On one WSI the confusion matrix is TP \(=805\), FN \(=18\), FP \(=48\), TN \(=614\); on all test WSIs it is TP \(=24\,796\), FN \(=4340\), FP \(=5345\), TN \(=158\,754\). Compute sensitivity, specificity, precision and accuracy for both. Then explain why patch-level metrics are not enough, how the FROC curve evaluates tumour detection, and what problems remained at the whole-slide level.
answer:
Definitions: sensitivity \(=\dfrac{TP}{TP+FN}\), specificity \(=\dfrac{TN}{TN+FP}\), precision \(=\dfrac{TP}{TP+FP}\), accuracy \(=\dfrac{TP+TN}{TP+FN+FP+TN}\).
Single WSI (1485 patches): sensitivity \(=805/823=\mathbf{0.978}\); specificity \(=614/662=\mathbf{0.927}\); precision \(=805/853=\mathbf{0.944}\); accuracy \(=1419/1485=\mathbf{0.956}\).
All test WSIs (193 235 patches): sensitivity \(=24\,796/29\,136=\mathbf{0.851}\); specificity \(=158\,754/164\,099=\mathbf{0.967}\); precision \(=24\,796/30\,141=\mathbf{0.823}\); accuracy \(=183\,550/193\,235=\mathbf{0.950}\).
Why not enough. These tile-based metrics answer "can we detect cancer in patches?", not whether a cancer (a tumour, a slide) will be detected. FROC evaluates the detection of particular tumours: for a threshold \(t\), sensitivity \(\approx\) the proportion of tumours containing at least one patch \(I\) with \(F(I)\ge t\) among all tumours in all slides, and AvgFP \(\approx\) the average number of patches with \(F(I)\ge t\) in each non-cancerous slide; varying \(t\) gives the curve.
Remaining issues: a WSI contains only cuts across tumours, so FROC is still limited; WSI-level evaluation needs huge numbers of WSIs; the system broke down on WSIs from a completely different scanner and hospital with slightly different colours – corrected by colour normalization, but more data from more hospitals is needed.
keyPoints: Single WSI: sensitivity 0.978, specificity 0.927, precision 0.944, accuracy 0.956
All WSIs: sensitivity 0.851, specificity 0.967, precision 0.823, accuracy 0.950
Patch metrics do not show whether tumours/slides are detected
FROC: tumour sensitivity vs average false-positive patches per non-cancerous slide, parametrized by the threshold \(t\)
WSI-level evaluation needs many WSIs
Domain shift (other scanner/hospital colours) → colour normalization, more data needed
source: PV021 L5 (inferred boundary), NN_2026_5.pdf, slides 192–195 (confusion matrices and FROC curve are figures on slides 192 and 194); sensitivity/specificity/precision/accuracy are standard definitions applied to the slide's matrices, not slide text
